title: PPDL: LLM-Based Flows as Probabilistic Programs
claim: Executing a flow probabilistically explores a distribution of traces, generalizing classical single-trace execution, and a single output can still be picked from it.
layout: Commutative-diagram square of 4 boxes, trace-graph insets at left and right edges
description: A square diagram of four light-blue boxes joined by thick black arrows with italic labels. The top-left box reads 'LLM-based flow with factors' and the top-right reads 'LLM-based flow'. The bottom-left reads 'distribution of output values' and the bottom-right reads 'single output value'. The top arrow is labeled 'ignore factors'. The left arrow is labeled 'probabilistically infer (explore trace distribution)'. The right arrow is labeled 'classically interpret (roll out single trace)'. The bottom arrow is labeled 'pick'. At the far left is a branching tree of gray circles, each circle an execution state, with darker shades meaning higher probability. At the far right is a single linear chain of circles. The contrast between the branching tree and the single chain shows the difference, and the eye lands first on the top-left box.
caption: Executing LLM-based flows with or without probabilistic programming. Each circle represents an execution state, with darker shades indicating higher normalized probability.
abstract: Building reliable applications that leverage large language models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge. While LLMs offer impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, their outputs often lack accuracy and provide no clear measure of confidence. This uncertainty compounds in flows of multiple calls to LLMs and other tools, making it difficult for developers and end-users to trust the results. This paper introduces a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows. It enables developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty throughout the application's flow, and experiment with different inference scaling techniques without adding a single line of code beyond the flow's logic. We present an experimental study to demonstrate this capability, and a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.
